stories.title: Fintech Firm More Than Doubles Footprint at 10 Astor Place
stories.excerpt: GFP Real Estate said Thursday that Maybern, a financial technology company specializing in fund management solutions for private markets, has signed a long-term lease expansion at 10 Astor Place, more than doubling its footprint at the property from approximately 11,000 square feet to 30,000 square feet. The expansion encompasses the property’s entire fourth floor. Maybern originally relocated to 10 Astor Place in 2024. Neith Stone of GFP Real Estate represented ownership, alongside Rob Silver, Anthony Sciacca and Brittany Silver of Newmark. Jonathan Franzel and Leo Kone of Newmark represented the tenant. “In today’s market, expansion tells a more meaningful story than relocation,” said Stone.  “When an existing tenant more than doubles its footprint and commits for the long term, it’s a powerful vote of confidence.  Tenants are drawn to boutique buildings like 10 Astor Place because they offer what new construction can’t replicate: enduring architecture, unmatched character and the kind of hands-on ownership today’s companies value.” The post Fintech Firm More Than Doubles Footprint at 10 Astor Place appeared first on Connect CRE.
bullets: Maybern fintech expands 11K to 30K SF at 10 Astor Place, NYC; long-term lease.
Tenant doubled footprint in under one year after 2024 relocation; full fourth floor takeover.
Boutique older buildings outcompete new construction for growing tech tenants seeking character, stability.
stories.summary: Maybern, a private-markets fund management fintech, more than doubled its footprint at 10 Astor Place in NoHo from 11,000 to 30,000 square feet on a long-term lease, occupying the entire fourth floor. The expansion signals tenant confidence and reflects preference for established, character-driven office buildings over new construction. Broker commentary emphasized that expansion (not relocation) conveys stronger market commitment.
stories.impact: Manhattan office: Growing fintech presence and rapid headcount expansion in NoHo/Flatiron corridor suggest sustained demand for smaller, trophy office assets in tech clusters. This may signal tight availability and pricing power for well-located Class B buildings, reducing cap rates and supporting new office-to-residential conversion projects in the submarket.

stories.title: Production Fabrication Firm Relocates to Rancho Dominguez
stories.excerpt: DAUM Commercial Real Estate Services completed a 10-year lease agreement for a 35,333 square-foot industrial property at 2945 East Maria St. in Rancho Dominguez on behalf of landlord Crown Associates Realty, Inc. The facility will serve as the West Coast operations hub for Cactus Fabrication, a company specializing in production fabrication for television, film and music videos. The new tenant is relocating from a smaller property in Los Angeles to better accommodate its growing operations, said Chuck Brill, an EVP and principal at DAUM who also serves as co-branch manager of the firm’s South Bay Office. “In addition to providing the larger footprint that the tenant requires, the asset’s quality, heavy electrical capacity, and functional layout featuring a large secured side yard and separate front-loading area is very well suited to their business needs,” Brill said. “Further, ownership has invested significantly in modernizing the building to like-new condition with superior office space, creating a true best-in-class industrial asset that will also act as a tool for attracting employees and creating a strong first impression for customers and business partners.” The post Production Fabrication Firm Relocates to Rancho Dominguez appeared first on Connect CRE.
bullets: Cactus Fabrication relocates TV/film production to 35.3K SF in Rancho Dominguez, LA; 10-year lease.
Tenant upsized from smaller LA property; requires heavy electrical, secured yard, modern office.
Industrial landlord modernized asset to attract growing operations needing employee/client-facing quality.
stories.summary: Cactus Fabrication, a production company serving television, film, and music video industries, signed a 10-year lease for a 35,333-square-foot industrial facility at 2945 East Maria Street in Rancho Dominguez, relocating from a smaller LA property. The landlord recently modernized the building with upgraded office space, heavy electrical capacity, and secure yard/loading areas tailored to production workflows. The relocation signals operational growth in the media/entertainment sector.
stories.impact: South Bay LA industrial: Media/entertainment production companies are consolidating into larger, modernized industrial assets near LA's media hubs. This indicates sustained demand for specialized industrial (not generic logistics) in Rancho Dominguez and suggests opportunity for developers to target industrial-to-mixed-use or creative-office conversions in the submarket as inventory remains tight.

In their expanded roles, Cruz, Harris and Jones will maintain their current project responsibilities while stepping into elevated leadership positions to shape the firm’s strategic direction, foster community-centered design and mentor emerging talent. Providence House has appointed Mary Brosnahan as its new CEO. The veteran nonprofit leader has spent more than three decades as a leading national voice on homelessness and housing instability. stories.title: Mermaid Inn Restaurateurs Ink 2K SF at 61 West 74th Street for New Eatery
stories.excerpt: Restaurateurs Danny Abrams and Cindy Smith are making a splash on the Upper West Side. The couple and co-founders of New England-style seafood spot Mermaid Inn have selected 61 West 74th Street for their next venture, Commercial Observer has learned. Abrams secured the 2,300-square-foot lease, plus a basement space, at $130 per square foot, according to broker Meridian Capital Group. The site, located between Columbus Avenue and Central Park West and about a block and a half south of Mermaid Inn, previously hosted Patsy’s Pizzeria. The locally beloved pizza joint permanently closed in January, citing the end of its lease and rising costs, West Side Rag reported. Counter Real Estate’s Justin Losh negotiated the new lease on behalf of the landlord, Viking Management. Meridian’s Carson Shahrabani and Noam Aziz represented Abrams. “Danny has an iconic restaurant, the Mermaid Inn, right around the corner, so it’s incredible to see him become the LeBron of the immediate neighborhood,” Shahrabani said in a statement to CO. The Upper West Side’s Mermaid Inn set up shop at 335 Columbus Avenue in 2024, after its longtime home along Amsterdam Avenue shuttered in 2022. Abrams and Smith operate a second Mermaid Inn location in Manhattan’s Chelsea neighborhood, as well as Mermaid Oyster Bar locations in Greenwich Village and Times Square. The upcoming restaurant at 61 West 74th Street remains unnamed and its concept undecided, according to Shahrabani. Abrams declined to share additional details on the new lease. Losh and Viking Management did not immediately respond to requests for comment. Emily Davis can be reached at edavis@commercialobserver.com.
bullets: Mermaid Inn restaurateurs lease 2.3K SF + basement at 61 West 74th, Manhattan; $130/SF.
Upper West Side location, one block south of original Mermaid Inn; replaces closed Patsy's Pizzeria.
Patsy's cited rising costs, lease end as closure reason; neighborhood restaurant expansion despite inflation.
stories.summary: Danny Abrams and Cindy Smith, founders of the Mermaid Inn seafood restaurant, signed a 2,300-square-foot lease plus basement space at 61 West 74th Street on the Upper West Side at $130 per square foot. The location, between Columbus and Central Park West, replaces Patsy's Pizzeria, which closed in January citing lease expiration and rising costs. The deal signals continued restaurant confidence in prime Manhattan neighborhoods.
stories.impact: Manhattan UWS retail/hospitality: Successful restaurant expansion at $130/SF despite cited cost pressures suggests strong tenant fundamentals and traffic in the submarket, but closure of competitor (Patsy's) due to rising rents signals margin pressure. Monitor if neighborhood retail recovers post-pandemic or if high rents compress F&B operators, affecting mixed-use development feasibility in UWS.

stories.title: Nordstrom Rack Takes 22K SF in Wellington, Fla.
stories.excerpt: nordstrom Rack has signed a 22,000-square-foot lease in Wellington, Fla., the Seattle-based retailer announced Thursday. Nordstrom Rack is the discount concept run by Nordstrom. The new store, set to open in spring 2027, will be at The Shoppes at Isla Verde at 800-1020 South State Road 7. Other tenants include Best Buy, Homesense, Total Wine & More, Petco, Old Navy, Ulta and Rack Room Shoes. Terms of the lease were not disclosed. MetLife Investment Management owns the shopping center, while Urban Retail Properties manages the property. MetLife acquired the 207,000-square-foot property in 2018 for $73.75 million, records show. The Shoppes at Isla Verde has experienced some tenant turnover in recent years. A Joann Fabrics store closed in 2025 as that retailer went out of business. According to bankruptcy filings, Joann Fabrics had occupied 21,600 square feet at the plaza since 2008. In another departure, organic grocer Sprouts closed its location at Shoppes at Isla Verde in 2023. Nordstrom Rack sells off-price apparel, accessories, beauty products, home decor and shoes. Nordstrom said it operates 23 Nordstrom Rack stores in Florida. Its Palm Beach County locations include stores in Palm Beach Gardens, West Palm Beach, Delray Beach and Boca Raton. Jeff Ostrowski can be reached at jostrowski@commercialobserver.com.
bullets: Nordstrom Rack opens 22K SF in Wellington, FL; spring 2027 opening at Shoppes at Isla Verde.
Center owned by MetLife, acquired 2018 for $73.75M; recent tenant churn (Joann, Sprouts closures).
Discount retail expansion into South Florida suburban power center despite prior vacancy.
stories.summary: Nordstrom Rack signed a 22,000-square-foot lease at The Shoppes at Isla Verde in Wellington, Florida, opening spring 2027. The 207,000-square-foot MetLife-owned shopping center has experienced recent tenant turnover: Joann Fabrics (21,600 SF) closed in 2025 during bankruptcy; Sprouts (organic grocer) closed in 2023. Co-tenants include Best Buy, Homesense, Total Wine, Petco, Old Navy, Ulta, and Rack Room Shoes.
stories.impact: South Florida retail/mixed-use: Nordstrom Rack's commitment signals stabilization at the center and confidence in Wellington's affluent suburban base, but prior closures (especially Joann's large footprint and Sprouts) indicate mixed retail fundamentals. For multifamily developers: monitor whether anchor retail strength translates to sustained traffic supporting residential components in mixed-use projects; consider that discount retail may underperform in high-barrier-to-entry markets.

stories.title: Immigration Law Firm Manifest Law Subleases 18K SF at 902 Broadway
stories.excerpt: The immigration attorneys at Manifest Law will be making some of their own moves, Commercial Observer has learned. The law firm signed a 18,200-square-foot sublease at Koeppel Rosen’s 902 Broadway, where it will be taking over space previously occupied by Adaptive Security, according to tenant brokerage Nomad Group. Asking rent for the space was $75 per square foot. Manifest Law will move into the entire eighth floor nearly four months after the artificial intelligence-powered cybersecurity company firm signed a 51,220-square-foot sublease of its own from BarkBox at Silverstein Properties’ 120 Broadway. 902 Broadway spans the length of Broadway between East 20th and East 21st streets, between the landmark Flatiron Building and Union Square. “Manifest’s move underscores Union Square and Flatiron’s emergence as a destination for ambitious AI companies committed to NYC and in-person collaboration,” Nomad’s Bill Janetschek, who represented Manifest Law alongside Nick Hein and Matthew DeRose, said in a statement. “Following its record-setting $60 million Series A, Manifest needed an HQ equal to its trajectory and a team capable of moving at its speed.” Christopher Foerch and Zev Holzman of Savills handled negotiation on behalf of Adaptive Security, but did not immediately respond to a request for comment. Manifest Law is relocating about five blocks from 333 Park Avenue South, according to Nomad Group. Other recent deals signed at 902 Broadway were for law firm Fenwick & West, which expanded to 72,800 square feet across four floors in June, and real estate development firm Hudson Companies taking 18,200 square feet in March. Mark Hallum can be reached at mhallum@commercialobserver.com.
bullets: Manifest Law subleases 18.2K SF at 902 Broadway (NoHo), takes full eighth floor.
Replaces Adaptive Security (AI cybersecurity); law firm relocating after $60M Series A fundraise.
Broker notes Union Square/Flatiron emergence as AI hub; in-person office demand post-remote.
AI employee platform Warp simultaneously tripled footprint to 24.5K SF at 156 Fifth (Flatiron).
stories.summary: Immigration law firm Manifest Law signed an 18,200-square-foot sublease of the entire eighth floor at 902 Broadway (Koeppel Rosen building, NoHo), replacing Adaptive Security, an AI-powered cybersecurity company that subleased from BarkBox. Manifest raised $60 million in Series A funding and sought HQ space matching its trajectory and emphasis on in-person collaboration. Broker commentary highlights Union Square and Flatiron as emerging AI/tech destination hubs.
stories.impact: Manhattan Flatiron/NoHo: Rapid office-space uptake by AI/tech firms (Manifest, Adaptive Security, Warp) signals strong venture-backed inflow, talent clustering, and preference for in-person collaborative workspaces despite remote-work trends. This concentration supports office scarcity and higher rents in the submarket, but may also accelerate future office-to-residential conversions if venture capital cycles slow. Multifamily developers should monitor AI company density and funding cycles as leading indicators of neighborhood desirability and renter demographic shifts (high-income, young knowledge workers).

stories.title: Starwood’s Net Income Drops 95% Annually — and Then Its Stock Drops
stories.excerpt: Starwood Property Trust’s stock tanked hours after the firm reported its second-quarter earnings, dropping 4 percent in one morning, as the firm reported major declines in net income. Starwood’s stock currently trades at $15.55 per share, down 6 percent from where it traded one month ago and down nearly 20 percent from a year ago. The Miami Beach-based lender and investment firm reported just $6.6 million in net income in the second quarter of 2026, an 87.3 percent decline from the $51.9 million it reported in the fourth quarter of 2025 and nearly 95 percent less than the $129.8 million in net income it reported in the second quarter of 2025. Distributable earnings totaled $151.5 million in the second quarter, up from $147.3 million in the previous quarter and $151.1 million this time last year. Chairman and CEO Barry Sternlicht said during the firm’s second-quarter earnings call Thursday that he was “a little surprised by the stock’s reaction this morning,” and insisted the firm’s foundation and fundamentals are strong. “I think we’re kind of throwing the baby out with the bathwater,” said Sternlicht, who noted that analysts seem concerned about the firm’s large loan lending and mortgage business. “We look at it differently: We’re pretty confident in our ability to get back to earnings power to drive the dividend and restore coverage of our dividend.” He noted that, at a property level, almost every asset class in the U.S. and Europe is “in repair, everything is getting better,” and particularly singled out equity real estate investment trusts in multifamily, self-storage, senior housing and logistics as showing positive signs. bullets: Starwood Property Trust Q2 2026 net income $6.6M, down 87% YoY and 95% vs Q2 2025.
Distributable earnings flat at $151.5M; stock down 4% day-of, 20% year-over-year.
CEO Sternlicht insists fundamentals strong; market reaction suggests investor concern on CRE lending outlook.
stories.summary: Starwood Property Trust reported Q2 2026 net income of $6.6 million, a steep 87% decline from Q4 2025 and nearly 95% lower than Q2 2025 ($129.8 million). Distributable earnings remained flat at $151.5 million year-over-year. Stock dropped 4% on earnings announcement and has declined 20% over the past year, trading at $15.55/share. CEO Barry Sternlicht defended the firm's fundamentals during the earnings call.
stories.impact: Broad CRE capital impact: Starwood's sharp net income collapse and stock decline signal stress in CRE lending and investment returns, likely reflecting higher losses on distressed assets, rates, and credit deterioration in the portfolio. For multifamily developers, this indicates tightening CRE lender profitability and potential pullback in construction lending, mezzanine, and bridge financing. Monitor Starwood's multifamily loan portfolio performance and watch for forced sales of REO apartments, which could add supply pressure and cap-rate compression in key markets.

stories.title: AI Employee Management Platform Warp Triples Footprint at 156 Fifth Avenue
stories.excerpt: Warp, an artificial intelligence-driven employee management platform, has more than tripled its office footprint for the second time in 12 months. The startup recently secured a 16,500-square-foot expansion to fully occupy the seventh floor at 156 Fifth Avenue, less than a year after settling at the Flatiron District building. Warp’s footprint now totals 24,500 square feet. The five-year deal carried an asking rent of $75 per square foot. The transaction brings 156 Fifth Avenue to 100 percent occupancy, according to Newmark’s Eric Cagner, who represented landlord HRC alongside Dylan Weisman, Leo Koné and Claire Koeppel. Warp signed its initial lease at 156 Fifth in the fall of 2025, taking 8,000 square feet on its eighth floor. That move quintupled Warp’s office footprint. It previously leased just 1,500 square feet at 14 East Fourth Street in NoHo. Warp has been full speed ahead ever since. Its most recent funding round raised $60 million, and subsequent headcount growth required a lot more elbow room. Current Real Estate Advisors’ Rob Kluge assisted Warp in its recent expansion. “I think that they thought that they would grow, but I don’t think they thought they would grow this quickly,” Kluge told Commercial Observer. “It was fortuitous timing that the floor below them was available.” HRC made upgrades to the seventh floor over the summer, prior to Warp taking occupancy in July. The landlord opened a new amenity space on the third floor, as well. “We are thrilled to see our existing tenant Warp continue to grow and to have been in a position where we could accommodate their needs,” Newmark’s Cagner said in a statement to CO. The possibility for future expansions at 156 Fifth Avenue cemented Warp’s decision to sustain growth inside the 13-story tower rather than look elsewhere, according to Kluge. bullets: Warp AI platform triples footprint to 24.5K SF at 156 Fifth Ave (Flatiron); second expansion in 12 months.
Raised $60M Series A; now occupies seventh and eighth floors; $75/SF asking rent.
Prior lease: 1.5K SF at NoHo (14 East Fourth); first 156 Fifth deal (8K SF, fall 2025) quintupled footprint.
stories.summary: Warp, an AI-driven employee management platform, expanded to 24,500 square feet at 156 Fifth Avenue in Flatiron, securing a 16,500-square-foot lease on the seventh floor at $75 per square foot on a five-year term. The expansion marks Warp's second major upsizing in 12 months: it initially leased 8,000 SF at 156 Fifth in fall 2025 (quintupling from 1,500 SF at 14 East Fourth in NoHo) and has now nearly tripled that footprint. Recent $60 million Series A funding drove rapid headcount growth.
stories.impact: Manhattan Flatiron office: Warp's explosive sequential expansion ($1.5K → $8K → $24.5K SF in 12 months) reflects venture-backed AI talent acquisition and in-person collaboration demand, filling 156 Fifth Avenue to 100% occupancy. This signals severe office scarcity and pricing power ($75/SF) in prime Flatiron for high-growth tech. For multifamily: AI company density, wage growth, and turnover in Flatiron/Union Square drive renter demand for premium residential in the submarket; monitor if office conversion accelerates if venture funding cycles cool.
